name: stalkerware-indicators
purpose: Curated indicator set for consumer stalkerware and monitoring apps — package names, certificates, network indicators and YARA rules — maintained for use with MVT and antivirus tooling.
journalism_use_case: Extends device checks beyond state-grade spyware to the commercial monitoring apps that are far more commonly used against journalists by employers, partners and local actors — a threat that MVT's mercenary-spyware indicators do not cover and that is statistically much more likely.
pros: Covers the threat most likely to be present on a journalist's device: commercial stalkerware is cheap, widely sold and used against individuals, unlike Pegasus-class implants
Designed to plug into MVT, so it extends an existing workflow rather than requiring a new one
Maintained by an organisation focused on technology-facilitated abuse, with current updates (pushed 2026-11-02) and a focused community (401 stars)
Includes network indicators and YARA rules as well as package names, so detection is multi-layered
cons: No licence detected by the GitHub API and none found in this survey — so redistribution and inclusion in a product are legally unresolved, which matters if you build internal tooling around it
Indicator lists are inherently incomplete and lag new stalkerware; a clean result is weak evidence of absence
No releases, so you track the default branch and cannot pin a verified indicator-set version — awkward for reproducible examinations
Detecting stalkerware on a device raises immediate safety questions (the installer often has physical access to the person) that are outside the tool's scope but inside yours
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 401 stars with 10 open issues, no releases, no detected licence, last push 2026-11-02. Échap's focus on technology-facilitated abuse is documented by the organisation; the indicator set is referenced in the stalkerware-detection community.
assessment: Use it alongside MVT — the coverage gap it fills is the one most likely to matter for an individual journalist. For your profile two points stand out. First, the unresolved licence means you should consume the indicators rather than redistribute them in a product, and ask Échap if you need clarity. Second, and more important: if a check finds stalkerware, the person's immediate physical safety may be at risk from whoever installed it, so have a safety plan and a referral route before you run the check, not after.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-02, no releases or tags, no detected licence, 401 stars, 10 open issues. Indicator updates within the last month from a focused organisation; maintenance assessed on update recency since indicator sets have no release cadence.
licence: NOT CONFIRMED — no licence detected by the GitHub API and no LICENSE file found (2026-11-17)
model_or_data_licence: Same — this is an indicator dataset, not software.
licence_restrictions: Unresolved. Consuming the indicators for your own examinations is the low-risk use; redistributing them or embedding them in a distributed product is legally unclear. Clarify with the maintainer if needed.
costs: No fee. Negligible — it is a data repository.
privacy: Static indicator data; using it discloses nothing. The sensitivity lies in the examination it supports, not the dataset.
alternatives: Amnesty International's published indicators of compromise for mercenary spyware
Exodus Privacy for tracker analysis of installed Android apps
Commercial anti-stalkerware products, which detect more but report to a vendor

name: Amnesty International investigations (indicators of compromise)
purpose: Repository of indicators of compromise published alongside Amnesty's technical investigations into mercenary spyware and targeted surveillance of civil society.
journalism_use_case: The authoritative indicator source for MVT checks: when Amnesty publishes an investigation into a new spyware campaign targeting journalists, the IOCs land here and can be fed directly into a device examination — which is how a newsroom keeps its device checks current rather than relying on last year's indicators.
pros: Authoritative provenance: these are the indicators from the investigations that publicly established spyware targeting of journalists, published by the organisation that did the forensic work
Designed to be consumed by MVT, so updating your detection capability is a matter of pulling new indicator files
Each indicator set is tied to a published investigation, so you can read the methodology behind the detection rather than trusting an opaque list
Public and free, which matters because commercial threat intelligence covering the same ground is expensive and not citable
cons: No licence detected in this survey, so redistribution terms are unresolved — a recurring problem with indicator repositories and a real constraint if you build tooling

Last push 2024-12-16: the repository is a publication archive rather than a continuously updated feed, so it is not a live indicator source and newer campaigns may be published elsewhere (for example in Security Lab reports directly)
Indicator-based detection only finds known campaigns; the absence of a match says nothing about a novel implant
No releases or versioning, so pinning an indicator-set state for a reproducible examination requires recording a commit hash yourself
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 1,733 stars with 6 open issues, no releases, no detected licence, last push 2024-12-16. Amnesty Security Lab's investigations are extensively documented publicly and are the basis of several confirmed cases of journalist targeting.
assessment: Essential as a reference and insufficient as your only indicator source, precisely because the repository has not been pushed in nearly two years — check securitylab.amnesty.org directly for newer publications rather than assuming this mirror is current. For your profile the practical arrangement is to pull indicators from here plus stalkerware-indicators, record the commit hashes used in each examination, and maintain a relationship with Amnesty Security Lab or Access Now for cases beyond your capacity, since they see campaigns before indicators are public.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2024-12-16, no releases, no detected licence, 1,733 stars, 6 open issues. Nearly two years since the last push. Classified stable-low rather than dormant because it is a publication archive tied to reports rather than a maintained feed — but it should not be treated as current indicator intelligence.
licence: NOT CONFIRMED — no licence detected by the GitHub API and no LICENSE file found (2026-11-17)
model_or_data_licence: Same — indicator data accompanying published research.
licence_restrictions: Unresolved. Consuming indicators for your own examinations is low risk; redistribution is unclear. Amnesty's published reports have their own terms.
privacy: Static data; consuming it discloses nothing (note that cloning from GitHub is visible to GitHub, which is unremarkable).
alternatives: securitylab.amnesty.org directly for the most current publications
stalkerware-indicators for consumer monitoring apps
Citizen Lab publications for additional campaign documentation

name: SpyGuard
purpose: Appliance-style tool that creates a Wi-Fi access point, captures a device's network traffic and analyses it against indicators of compromise to detect spyware communication, without installing anything on the device.
journalism_use_case: Non-invasive device screening: a journalist connects their phone to a SpyGuard access point for a few minutes and the traffic is analysed for known spyware command-and-control communication — no backup, no ADB, nothing installed, which makes it usable in a workshop or a field setting where MVT's acquisition is impractical.
pros: Requires nothing on the device, which is a genuine advantage for consent, speed and for devices you cannot or should not back up — a workshop can screen a dozen phones in an hour
Network-level detection catches active communication that an on-device check might miss, so it is complementary to MVT rather than duplicative
Apache-2.0 — a clean OSI licence, notably unlike MVT's consensual-use restriction, so there is no licensing complication
Fork of Kaspersky's TinyCheck (whose original repository is now a 404, verified in this session), so this is the surviving maintained line of a well-regarded design
cons: Only detects spyware that communicates during the capture window, so a dormant implant or one using a novel endpoint is invisible — a clean result is weak evidence
Indicator-dependent like all such tooling, and the indicator sets age
Requires dedicated hardware (a Raspberry Pi class device with two network interfaces) and setup, so it is an appliance to build rather than software to install
Slowing cadence: release v2.1 and last push both 2026-06-16, five months before this survey, with 514 stars and 13 open issues
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 514 stars with 13 open issues, release v2.1 (2026-06-16) with the last push the same day, Apache-2.0. Its lineage from Kaspersky's TinyCheck is stated by the project, and the original KasperskyLab/TinyCheck path returns a 404 (verified 2026-11-17) — making SpyGuard the available implementation.
assessment: Worth building as an appliance if you run digital-security workshops or support journalists in the field — the non-invasive screening model fits those settings far better than MVT. For your profile I would treat it as triage rather than examination: a hit justifies a full MVT examination, and a clean result justifies nothing beyond 'no known spyware communicated in those minutes'. Keep the indicator sets updated and note the slowing maintenance as a monitoring item.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-06-16, latest release v2.1 published the same day, 514 stars, 13 open issues. Five months since any activity on a security tool whose value depends on current indicators — a real caveat, though the project is complete rather than abandoned.
model_or_data_licence: Indicator sets come from third-party sources with their own terms.
licence_restrictions: None material — a clean OSI licence, which is a notable contrast with MVT in the same workflow.
costs: No fee. Hardware: a Raspberry Pi class device with two network interfaces plus a screen or remote access (low hundreds in hardware, estimate). Build and maintenance time for the appliance.
privacy: Traffic capture happens on your appliance and stays there; nothing is sent to a vendor. The captured traffic is highly sensitive (it is the person's live network activity), so retention should be minimal and consent explicit even though the licence does not compel it.
alternatives: MVT for a deeper on-device examination
Pi-hole or a manual pcap plus indicator matching for a do-it-yourself equivalent
Referral to Access Now's Digital Security Helpline for individual cases
summary: Appliance-style tool that creates a Wi-Fi access point, captures a device's network traffic and analyses it against indicators of…

name: EFF Rayhunter
purpose: Rust application that runs on an inexpensive mobile hotspot to analyse the cellular control plane and detect behaviour characteristic of cell-site simulators (IMSI catchers), such as downgrade attacks and unusual identity requests.
journalism_use_case: Detecting whether a protest, a courthouse, a border crossing or a newsroom's surroundings are being surveilled with an IMSI catcher — a question journalists have had no practical way to answer, and one that is both a protective measure and, when a detection occurs, a story in itself.
pros: Addresses a surveillance technique that was effectively undetectable by journalists until now, and does so on hardware costing tens rather than thousands — a genuine capability change for the field
Dual value: protective (know when your communications are being intercepted) and investigative (document that a specific location was surveilled at a specific time)
GPL-3.0, very actively maintained (v0.13.0, 2026-09-16; pushed 2026-11-17) with 6,069 stars and EFF's institutional backing and legal literacy
Runs on specific inexpensive hotspot hardware, so a newsroom can deploy several and build a picture over time
cons: Detections are heuristic signals about anomalous network behaviour, not proof that a cell-site simulator was present — and publishing 'an IMSI catcher was deployed' on a heuristic alone would be a serious overreach
Requires specific supported hotspot hardware, and the supported-device list is a procurement constraint that varies by region and carrier bands
Cellular-network behaviour varies legitimately by carrier and location, so baselining is necessary before anomalies mean anything — and that takes time and local knowledge
GPL-3.0 and 6,069 stars indicate a young, rapidly developing project, so expect behaviour changes between versions and keep notes on which version produced which detection
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 6,069 stars with release v0.13.0 (2026-09-16) and a push on 2026-11-17, GPL-3.0, maintained by EFF. The rapid growth in stars for a hardware-dependent tool indicates substantial interest in the capability; EFF publishes guidance on interpreting results, which is the relevant support context.
assessment: Adopt it — this is one of the most interesting items in the whole catalogue for your context, because it converts an invisible threat into something observable and reportable. Two disciplines are essential. First, baseline normal cellular behaviour in your locations before treating anomalies as detections, otherwise you will produce false alarms. Second, in published work describe what was observed (specific control-plane anomalies, at a time and place) rather than asserting the presence of a device, and get a cellular-security expert to review before publication. Deploy several units if protest or courthouse coverage is a regular beat.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-17, latest release v0.13.0 (2026-09-16), 6,069 stars, GPL-3.0. Same-day commits with frequent releases under EFF's institutional maintenance; a young project with strong momentum.
licence_restrictions: GPL-3.0; immaterial for internal use. Note that operating cellular-monitoring equipment may engage local radio or wiretapping law — a legal question entirely separate from the licence, and one to check in each jurisdiction where you deploy.
costs: No software fee. Hardware: a supported mobile hotspot (low tens to low hundreds, estimate) per deployment plus a mobile data plan if you want it operating in the field. Among the best capability-per-cost items in the catalogue.
privacy: Analysis is local on the device; nothing is transmitted to EFF. The data collected is about the network rather than about individuals, which keeps the privacy profile clean. Possession and operation of the device may itself attract attention in a hostile jurisdiction.
alternatives: Commercial IMSI-catcher detection products, which are expensive and opaque
Crowdsourced cell-tower databases (OpenCellID) for corroborating anomalies against known infrastructure
SnoopSnitch and similar Android apps, with narrower device support
blockers: Requires specific supported hotspot hardware; operating cellular monitoring may engage local radio law
summary: Rust application that runs on an inexpensive mobile hotspot to analyse the cellular control plane and detect behaviour…

name: libimobiledevice
purpose: Cross-platform protocol library and tools for communicating with iOS devices without jailbreaking — creating backups, reading device information, mounting filesystems and accessing diagnostic services.
journalism_use_case: The acquisition layer for iOS device checks on Linux: create the encrypted backup that MVT analyses, read device identifiers and diagnostics, and do it from a forensic workstation rather than requiring macOS and iTunes.
pros: Enables iOS forensic acquisition on Linux, which is what makes a dedicated forensic workstation (rather than a journalist's Mac) practical — a meaningful operational-security improvement
Reverse-engineered protocol implementation maintained over many years, with very active development (pushed 2026-11-17) and a large user base (8,352 stars)
LGPL-2.1, so it can be linked from your own tooling without copyleft contamination
Underpins MVT's iOS workflow, so it is a dependency you will have whether you install it deliberately or not
cons: 850 open issues — by far the largest backlog in this segment — reflecting the difficulty of tracking Apple's protocol changes across iOS versions
Breakage after iOS releases is a recurring pattern: a new iOS version can render acquisition unreliable until the library catches up, which is exactly when you may need it
Release cadence lags development (1.4.0 from 2025-10-10 against commits in November 2026), so you often need to build from source
Low-level and engineer-facing; errors are cryptic and diagnosing a failed acquisition takes experience
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 8,352 stars with 850 open issues, release 1.4.0 (2025-10-10), pushed 2026-11-17, LGPL-2.1. The large backlog alongside daily commits is characteristic of a reverse-engineering project chasing a moving proprietary target.
assessment: Adopt as infrastructure for iOS device checks, and plan around the iOS-version lag: keep a note of which library version successfully acquired from which iOS version, and expect to build from source after a major iOS release. For your profile the broader point is that iOS acquisition capability is a dependency on a volunteer reverse-engineering effort — worth supporting, and worth having a fallback (a macOS machine for backups) when a check cannot wait for the library to catch up.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-17, latest release 1.4.0 (2025-10-10), 8,352 stars, 850 open issues. Same-day commits with infrequent releases; the backlog is intrinsic to chasing Apple's undocumented protocols rather than evidence of neglect.
licence_restrictions: LGPL-2.1 permits linking from your own tooling provided the library remains replaceable; modifications must be shared.
costs: No fee. A Linux forensic workstation and storage for backups (tens of GB per device). Build-from-source effort is the hidden cost.
privacy: Entirely local device communication; nothing is transmitted. The backups it creates are extremely sensitive and should be encrypted at rest with a short retention period.
alternatives: macOS Finder/iTunes backups where a Mac is available and acceptable
iLEAPP for parsing the acquired data
Commercial forensic suites (Cellebrite class) — avoid for journalist device checks: expensive, vendor-dependent and inappropriate for a consent-based protective examination
summary: Cross-platform protocol library and tools for communicating with iOS devices without jailbreaking — creating backups…

name: iLEAPP
purpose: iOS Logs, Events And Plist Parser: processes iOS backups and filesystem extractions into readable reports covering app usage, locations, connections, notifications, installed applications and hundreds of other artefact types.
journalism_use_case: Going beyond spyware indicators to understand what actually happened on a device: when a journalist believes their phone was accessed at a border crossing, iLEAPP's artefact timeline — unlocks, connections, app launches, file access — is how you establish what was done and when.
pros: Breadth of artefact coverage is the point: hundreds of parsers mean you can reconstruct device activity in detail rather than only checking for known malware, which is what a 'was my phone searched?' question requires
MIT licensed and extremely actively maintained (v2026.4.6, 2026-11-03; pushed 2026-11-17) with a healthy tracker (48 open issues against 1,452 stars)
Produces HTML and structured reports usable by a non-forensic colleague, which matters when explaining findings to a journalist or a lawyer
Community-driven parser contributions mean coverage of new iOS artefacts appears quickly
cons: Interpretation is the hard part and the tool does not help with it: an artefact timeline is extremely easy to over-read, and attributing an event to a hostile actor rather than ordinary device behaviour requires real expertise
Output volume is large — hundreds of artefact categories — so triage skill determines whether an examination is useful or just exhausting
Designed for law-enforcement-style forensics, so the framing and defaults assume an investigative rather than protective context; the ethical posture is yours to supply
Requires a prior acquisition (libimobiledevice or a macOS backup), so it is one stage of a chain
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 1,452 stars with 48 open issues, release v2026.4.6 (2026-11-03), pushed 2026-11-17, MIT licence. iLEAPP is widely used in the digital-forensics community, which is relevant adjacent credibility; its journalism use is not separately evidenced here.
assessment: Adopt for the specific case where you need to know what happened on a device rather than merely whether known spyware is present — border searches, suspected physical access, device handover after detention. For your profile the limiting factor is expertise, not tooling: budget for forensic training or a relationship with a practitioner, because an over-read timeline presented to a frightened journalist does harm. Pair with MVT (indicators) and document consent as you would for MVT even though the licence does not require it.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-17, latest release v2026.4.6 (2026-11-03), 1,452 stars, 48 open issues. Same-day commits with date-versioned releases; a very active community-contributed parser ecosystem.
licence_restrictions: None material — notably unrestricted compared with MVT in the same workflow.
costs: No fee. A forensic workstation and storage. The dominant cost is analyst expertise and time per examination. Estimate.
privacy: Local processing of an acquired backup. The data is the most sensitive you will handle — full device activity history — so encryption at rest, minimal retention, documented disposal and restricted access are essential regardless of licence requirements.
alternatives: MVT for spyware-indicator checks specifically
ALEAPP for the Android equivalent
A professional forensic practitioner where the stakes or the complexity are high
summary: iOS Logs, Events And Plist Parser: processes iOS backups and filesystem extractions into readable reports covering app usage…

name: ALEAPP
purpose: Android Logs Events And Protobuf Parser: processes Android extractions into readable reports across app usage, locations, accounts, connections, notifications and many other artefact types.
journalism_use_case: The Android counterpart for understanding device activity after a suspected search, seizure or unauthorised access — reconstructing what applications ran, what accounts were present and what connections were made, from an androidqf or filesystem extraction.
pros: Fills the Android gap that matters because Android is the dominant platform for journalists in much of the world, where iOS-centric tooling leaves them unserved
MIT licensed with very active maintenance (v2026.4.5, 2026-11-03; pushed 2026-11-17) and a healthy tracker (37 open issues)
Same reporting model as iLEAPP, so an analyst learns one workflow for both platforms
Community parser contributions keep pace with Android's rapid artefact changes
cons: Android artefact availability depends heavily on what the acquisition captured, which without root is substantially less than an iOS backup — so reports are thinner and gaps are common
Android fragmentation across vendors and versions means parser coverage is uneven: a Chinese-market device may yield far less than a Pixel
Same interpretation risk as iLEAPP, amplified by sparser data — fewer artefacts make over-reading more likely
Requires a prior acquisition step and forensic literacy; not usable by a journalist directly
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 1,052 stars with 37 open issues, release v2026.4.5 (2026-11-03), pushed 2026-11-17, MIT licence. Widely used in the digital-forensics community alongside iLEAPP.
assessment: Adopt alongside androidqf for Android cases, with realistic expectations: the examination will be shallower than an iOS one and you should say so when reporting a result. For your profile the honest framing for Android users is that protective examination is less capable on their platform, which should influence advice — a journalist at high risk may be better served by a well-configured iPhone or GrapheneOS device than by a stock Android phone you can only partially examine.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-17, latest release v2026.4.5 (2026-11-03), 1,052 stars, 37 open issues. Same-day commits with date-versioned releases from an active maintainer and contributor community.
costs: No fee. Workstation and storage; analyst time dominates. Estimate.
privacy: Local processing of acquired data, which is highly sensitive personal information requiring encrypted storage, minimal retention and documented disposal.
alternatives: androidqf plus MVT for indicator-focused checks
iLEAPP for the iOS equivalent
Autopsy for a broader forensic platform with a graphical interface
summary: Android Logs Events And Protobuf Parser: processes Android extractions into readable reports across app usage, locations…

name: Andriller
purpose: Collection of forensic tools for Android devices with a graphical interface, performing data extraction, lock-screen cracking for older devices and decoding of application databases into reports.
journalism_use_case: Historically a graphical alternative for Android extraction and app-database decoding, usable by someone without command-line forensics experience — relevant now mainly as a reference point when evaluating what a GUI-driven Android examination would look like.
pros: Graphical interface lowered the barrier for Android examination relative to CLI tooling, which was its main contribution
Application-database decoders covered messaging and social apps in a form directly useful to an investigator
MIT licensed with a sizeable historical community (1,633 stars) and a clean issue tracker at the point it stopped
cons: DORMANT: last push 2022-06-27 and release 3.6.3 (2022-04-30) — over four years without activity, during which Android's security model, app database formats and ADB behaviour have all changed substantially
Android forensics is the fastest-moving area in this segment, so a four-year-old tool's decoders are substantially obsolete
Lock-screen cracking features target old Android versions and are irrelevant to current devices, while potentially raising legal questions about use
Unmaintained security-adjacent software on a forensic workstation is itself a risk
feedback: No individual user reports verified. Documented: 1,633 stars with 13 open issues, release 3.6.3 (2022-04-30), last push 2022-06-27, MIT licence. The four-year gap is decisive given the pace of change in Android internals.
assessment: Avoid for new deployment — ALEAPP plus androidqf covers the same ground with current parsers and active maintenance. The reason to keep it in the catalogue is that it still appears in digital-forensics tool lists and training material, and anyone following those recommendations should know it has not been maintained since 2022. If a GUI is genuinely required for your analysts, Autopsy is the maintained option.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2022-06-27, latest release 3.6.3 (2022-04-30), 1,633 stars, 13 open issues. Over four years inactive in the fastest-changing area of mobile forensics.
licence_restrictions: None, but the code is stale.
costs: No fee. Not worth the deployment effort.
privacy: Local processing. Running unmaintained forensic software on a workstation handling sensitive device data is itself a security consideration.
alternatives: ALEAPP — recommended: current Android artefact parsing, actively maintained
androidqf for acquisition
Autopsy where a graphical forensic platform is required
blockers: Dormant since 2022; Android internals have changed substantially since
summary: Collection of forensic tools for Android devices with a graphical interface, performing data extraction…

name: Autopsy
purpose: Graphical digital-forensics platform built on The Sleuth Kit, providing disk-image analysis, timeline reconstruction, keyword search, file carving, hash matching and extensible modules.
journalism_use_case: Examining computers rather than phones: analysing a disk image from a laptop that may have been tampered with during a border crossing, reconstructing a timeline of file access on a device handed over by a source, or carving deleted documents from a drive that forms part of a leak.
pros: The standard open forensic platform for disk analysis, with timeline reconstruction and file carving that have no real open alternative at this level of maturity
Graphical interface and case-management model make it usable by an analyst without command-line forensics fluency, and reports are presentable to lawyers
Extensible module system, so you can add keyword lists or hash sets specific to an investigation
Long institutional history with a release in 2026 (autopsy-4.23.1, 2026-05-07) and a substantial community (3,455 stars)
cons: Slowing cadence and a large backlog: last push 2026-06-20 with 406 open issues, and no SPDX licence detected by the GitHub API (the project is Apache-2.0 per its own documentation, but this needed resolving rather than assuming)
Java desktop application with a heavy footprint and a Windows-first orientation; Linux use is possible but less smooth
Designed for law-enforcement workflows, so the framing assumes an adversarial investigation of a device owner rather than a protective examination for them — the ethics are yours to impose
Disk forensics requires real expertise, and the gap between running Autopsy and producing a defensible finding is large
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 3,455 stars with 406 open issues, release autopsy-4.23.1 (2026-05-07), last push 2026-06-20, no SPDX detected. Autopsy's standing in digital forensics is well established; its journalism use is not separately evidenced here.
assessment: Keep it available for computer rather than phone examinations, which is a less frequent but real need — particularly device-tampering questions after travel or detention. For your profile I would not build in-house disk-forensics capability unless the need recurs; the expertise threshold is high and a practitioner relationship is usually better value. Where you do use it, work from a verified image of the drive and never from the original, and document the hash chain.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-06-20, latest release autopsy-4.23.1 (2026-05-07), no SPDX detected, 3,455 stars, 406 open issues. Five months since last push with a 2026 release; a mature platform at reduced velocity with a substantial backlog.
licence: Apache-2.0 per the project's own documentation; GitHub API reports no detected licence (confirm the LICENSE file for compliance records)
model_or_data_licence: n/a. Hash sets and keyword lists you import carry their own terms.
licence_restrictions: None material if Apache-2.0 as documented; verify the licence file before redistributing a bundled product.
costs: No fee. A workstation with substantial disk for images (a full disk image is the size of the drive) and RAM. Commercial support and training are available from the vendor at prices not verified here.
privacy: Local analysis. Disk images contain everything on a device, so handling obligations are at the highest level: encrypted storage, access control, documented retention and disposal.
alternatives: The Sleuth Kit command-line tools for scripted analysis
A professional forensic practitioner for high-stakes device-tampering questions
iLEAPP/ALEAPP where the device is a phone rather than a computer
summary: Graphical digital-forensics platform built on The Sleuth Kit, providing disk-image analysis, timeline reconstruction…
